entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier series coefficients of a sine wave by converting it into positive and negative fundamental-frequency complex exponentials and identifying the nonzero harmonic coefficients that determine its magnitude and phase spectra.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Coefficients of a Sine Wave
sections.learning_goal: Set up the complex Fourier series form of a sine wave and show that only the $k=\pm1$ harmonics are present in the unit-amplitude zero-phase case.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this step is symbolic only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The lesson uses algebraic decomposition only.

question_policy.answer_format: No practice questions in the tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how Euler's formula turns $\sin(\omega_0 t)$ into the two harmonic terms at $k=1$ and $k=-1$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use the unit-amplitude, zero-phase sine wave $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$ with period $T_0=2\pi/\omega_0$.
paragraph_plan: State the Fourier series target form $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}$ and explain that a sine wave should occupy only two harmonic slots.
Introduce Euler's identity for sine and write the sine wave as a difference of positive and negative fundamental-frequency exponentials.
Match each exponential term to the $k=1$ and $k=-1$ basis functions.
Read off the two nonzero coefficients and note that every other $c_k$ is zero.
Close by previewing how amplitude and phase changes will simply rescale or rotate the same two coefficients.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable; this section is a tutorial.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation compact, keep all notation symbolic, and end by naming the sparse $k=\pm1$ coefficient pattern.

sections.section_title: Converting a Sine Wave into Complex Exponentials
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite a sine wave as positive and negative complex exponentials at the fundamental frequency.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this step is symbolic only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The worked example is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; one equivalent exponential-form rewrite.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which exponential rewrite is equivalent to a sine wave at the fundamental frequency.
distractor_plan: Use cosine-form answers instead of sine-form exponentials.
Flip the sign of the $j$ denominator or move the minus sign to the wrong term.
Omit one of the two exponentials or keep only the positive-frequency term.
Use the wrong harmonic frequency, such as $e^{j2\omega_0 t}$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is a worked example that starts with the algebraic rewrite.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=\sin(\omega_0 t)$ as a sum of positive and negative fundamental-frequency complex exponentials.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert the sine into two exponential terms and make the $k=1$ and $k=-1$ harmonics explicit.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the guided tutorial derivation to an explicit algebraic rewrite problem with the same base sine wave.
solution_step_plan: Write the Euler identity for sine.
Substitute $\theta=\omega_0 t$ and split the signal into a positive-frequency term and a negative-frequency term.
Match each term to the $k=1$ and $k=-1$ harmonic basis function.
State the rewritten sine wave in exponential form without introducing any extra harmonics.
practice_variation_axes: Change the sign of the sine wave.
Change the harmonic frequency while keeping the same rewrite pattern.
Rewrite a numerically scaled sine wave as the same exponential pair.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example short; the point is the exponential rewrite, not coefficient extraction yet.

sections.section_title: Identifying the k = 1 and k = -1 Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Read the $k=1$ and $k=-1$ coefficient values directly from the exponential form of a sine wave.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this step is symbolic only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The task is coefficient identification from notation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices giving the coefficient pair or a statement about which coefficients are nonzero.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which pair of coefficients belongs to the $k=\pm1$ slots after the sine has been rewritten as exponentials.
distractor_plan: Swap the $k=1$ and $k=-1$ coefficients.
Simplify $1/(2j)$ incorrectly into $1/2$ or $j/2$.
Add an unsupported DC term.
Claim that a higher harmonic is nonzero.
Treat the sine like a cosine and introduce real coefficients.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is a worked example that starts from the coefficient form.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=\frac{1}{2j}e^{j\omega_0 t}-\frac{1}{2j}e^{-j\omega_0 t}$, identify the nonzero Fourier coefficients.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Extract $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$, simplify them into rectangular form if useful, and state that all other coefficients are zero.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Starts from the rewritten exponential form and asks the learner to map each term to the correct coefficient slot.
solution_step_plan: Match the positive-frequency exponential to $c_1$.
Match the negative-frequency exponential to $c_{-1}$.
Simplify the coefficients into rectangular form if needed.
State that every other $c_k$ is zero because no other harmonics appear.
practice_variation_axes: Present the coefficients in rectangular form instead of exponential form.
Reverse the sign of the sine wave.
Include a zero coefficient distractor for $k=0$ or $k=2$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the relationship between the two coefficients explicit and do not introduce amplitude or phase yet.

sections.section_title: Including Amplitude in Sine-Wave Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Scale the nonzero Fourier coefficients when the sine wave amplitude changes.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this step is symbolic only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The example only rescales the symbolic coefficients.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices giving the amplitude-scaled coefficient pair.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which coefficient pair matches an amplitude-scaled sine wave.
distractor_plan: Forget to scale the coefficients by the amplitude.
Scale only one harmonic instead of both.
Create a DC coefficient that should not be present.
Drop the factor of $j$ or flip its sign.
Confuse amplitude scaling with phase rotation.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is a worked example that starts from an amplitude-scaled sine wave.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the complex Fourier coefficients of $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Multiply the unit-sine coefficient pair by $A$ and keep only the $k=\pm1$ terms.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds an amplitude factor while keeping the same harmonic structure.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite the sine with Euler's formula.
Factor the amplitude $A$ through the exponential pair.
Scale the $k=1$ and $k=-1$ coefficients by $A$.
State that no other coefficients change from the unit-amplitude case.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive and negative amplitudes.
Use fractional amplitudes.
Keep the same frequency but vary the numerical scale.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the algebra one step beyond the previous example: same pattern, just scaled by $A$.

sections.section_title: Including Sinusoidal Phase in the Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Carry a phase shift through the sine-to-exponential rewrite and identify the phase-rotated coefficients.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this step is symbolic only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The example is a phase-rotation of the same coefficient pattern.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices giving the phase-shifted coefficient pair.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which coefficient pair matches a phase-shifted sine wave.
distractor_plan: Put the same phase factor on both coefficients.
Put the phase on the wrong harmonic.
Treat phase as a magnitude change.
Lose the opposite-sign relationship between the two coefficients.
Forget the factor of $A$ when amplitude and phase both appear.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is a worked example that starts from a phase-shifted sine wave.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the complex Fourier coefficients of $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Separate the phase factor into $e^{\pm j\phi}$ terms and read off the rotated $k=\pm1$ coefficients.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces sinusoidal phase so the coefficient pair acquires opposite complex phase factors.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite $\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)$ with Euler's formula.
Factor the phase term out of each exponential.
Identify the $k=1$ coefficient and the $k=-1$ coefficient with their phase factors intact.
Keep the zero-coefficient pattern for all other harmonics.
practice_variation_axes: Change the phase angle $\phi$.
Use a negative phase shift.
Combine amplitude and phase changes in the same prompt.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that the phase shift creates complex rotation, not a new harmonic pattern.

sections.section_title: Reading Magnitude and Phase from Sine-Wave Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Read magnitude and phase information from the nonzero Fourier coefficients of a sine wave.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; this step is symbolic only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The step interprets coefficients symbolically as spectra.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices describing the magnitude/phase pattern of the nonzero harmonics.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask which magnitude/phase spectrum description matches a sine wave's coefficient pair.
distractor_plan: Report coefficient values instead of magnitudes.
Omit the $k=-1$ line.
Mistake the phase of $1/j$ for $+\pi/2$ instead of $-\pi/2$.
Include DC or higher harmonics that are actually zero.
Confuse phase spectrum with amplitude scaling.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is a worked example that starts from the coefficient pair and reads the spectrum.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: From the coefficients of $x(t)=A\sin(\omega_0 t+\phi)$, determine the magnitude and phase spectrum entries at $k=\pm1$ and state which harmonics are nonzero.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute $|c_{\pm1}|=A/2$, extract the corresponding arguments, and identify the sparse spectral lines.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from coefficient computation to the spectral interpretation of those coefficients.
solution_step_plan: Compute the magnitudes of the two nonzero coefficients.
Extract the principal-value arguments of the coefficients.
Place nonzero lines only at $k=\pm1$ in the spectrum interpretation.
State the magnitude and phase pattern that corresponds to the sine wave.

entries.lesson_title: Fourier Coefficients of a Rectangular Periodic Signal
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the complex Fourier series coefficients of a rectangular periodic signal by recognizing that only the pulse-support interval contributes to the one-period coefficient integral and evaluating the resulting exponential integral in terms of amplitude, width, period, and harmonic index.

sections.learning_goal: Introduce the one-period coefficient formula for a rectangular periodic signal and show that only the pulse-support interval contributes.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

paragraph_plan: State the complex Fourier coefficient formula for one period and name the rectangular signal parameters $A$, $\tau$, and $T$.

sections.section_title: Reading Amplitude, Pulse Width, and Period from a Rectangular Signal
sections.learning_goal: Read amplitude, pulse width, and period directly from a rectangular signal plot and translate the visual data into $A$, $\tau$, and $T$.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a rectangular periodic signal plot, identify the amplitude $A$, pulse width $\tau$, and period $T$ from the visual data.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the abstract coefficient setup to a concrete visual signal with readable amplitude, width, and period.
solution_step_plan: Read the peak value of the rectangle as the amplitude $A$.
Measure the horizontal extent of one pulse as the pulse width $\tau$.
Measure the spacing between repeated pulses as the period $T$.

period

sections.section_title: Restricting the Coefficient Integral to the Pulse Support
sections.learning_goal: Restrict the one-period coefficient integral to the pulse-support interval and factor out the constant amplitude.

question_policy.answer_format: restricted integral expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ on the rest of each period $T$, choose the correct coefficient integral after restricting to the pulse support.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the parameter-reading result as a piecewise signal definition and converts it into the restricted integral.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Exponential Integral for Nonzero Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate the restricted exponential integral for a specific nonzero harmonic and simplify the coefficient.

question_policy.answer_format: complex coefficient value or symbolic exponential expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Compute the value of a nonzero-harmonic coefficient after setting up the restricted integral for a rectangular periodic signal.

lose the negative sign from the exponential antiderivative
forget the $1/T$ factor in front of the integral
evaluate the exponential at the wrong bounds

example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one specific nonzero harmonic after the support restriction instead of leaving $k$ symbolic.

Integrate $e^{-j\omega_0 t}$ over the pulse-support interval.
Evaluate the antiderivative at the pulse endpoints.
Simplify the result into the standard nonzero-harmonic form.

sections.section_title: Writing Rectangular-Signal Coefficients Using Amplitude, Width, Period, and Harmonic Index
sections.learning_goal: Write the general complex Fourier coefficient formula for a rectangular periodic signal in terms of $A$, $\tau$, $T$, and $k$.

question_policy.answer_format: symbolic coefficient formula
question_policy.practice_question_model: Choose the correct general formula for $c_k$ of a rectangular periodic signal and separate the $k=0$ case from the $k\ne0$ case.
distractor_plan: omit the special $k=0$ case
swap $\tau$ and $T$ in the exponent or denominator
leave out the amplitude factor $A$
use the wrong sign in the exponential difference
state only the nonzero-harmonic case and ignore the DC coefficient

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For a rectangular periodic signal that equals $A$ on $0\le t<\tau$ and $0$ otherwise over period $T$, write the formula for $c_k$ and separate the $k=0$ case from the $k\ne0$ case.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the general coefficient formula with the DC coefficient $c_0=\frac{A\tau}{T}$ and the nonzero-harmonic expression $c_k=\frac{A}{-jk\omega_0 T}\left(e^{-jk\omega_0\tau}-1\right)$ for $k\ne0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Removes the specific harmonic index and turns the same computation into the reusable closed form.
solution_step_plan: Start from the restricted coefficient integral on the pulse-support interval.
Evaluate the exponential antiderivative symbolically.
Substitute $\omega_0=2\pi/T$ to express the result in period-based form.
Separate the $k=0$ average-value term from the $k\ne0$ harmonic term.
Write the final piecewise formula for all $k$.
practice_variation_axes: symbolic parameter values
harmonic index $k$
whether the prompt asks for $c_0$, $c_k$ with $k\ne0$, or both
whether the answer is requested in terms of $\omega_0$ or $T$

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC Fourier-series coefficient for a rectangular periodic signal by converting duty cycle and signal levels into the average value over one period.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Duty Cycle and DC Value
sections.learning_goal: Establish the DC value as the one-period average for a rectangular periodic signal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the signal is described symbolically with duty cycle, period, and level values.

question_policy.answer_format: Not applicable; this section is tutorial only.
question_policy.practice_question_model: No questions in the tutorial. Move directly from the definition of duty cycle to the average-value idea.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define duty cycle $D$ and show that the DC value is the one-period average. Start with the simplest rectangular pulse train so the learner can compute the average before any two-level generalization.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A signal equals $A$ on one interval of length $\tau$ inside a period $T$, and $0$ elsewhere.
paragraph_plan: State that the DC value is the average over one period and introduce duty cycle as $D = \tau/T$.
Write the average as an integral over one period and connect it to the rectangular pulse area.
Work the base case with high level $A$ and low level $0$ to obtain the DC value $A D$.
Close by signaling that the same averaging idea will handle later examples with different signal levels.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the instruction definition-first and compact. Do not introduce the two-level weighted average until the examples.

sections.section_title: Computing DC Value from a Given Duty Cycle
sections.learning_goal: Apply the duty-cycle average formula when the duty cycle is already given.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the prompt is fully symbolic with duty cycle and levels in text.

question_policy.answer_format: A single simplified symbolic value or fraction for the DC value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A rectangular signal is $A$ for a fraction $D$ of each period and $0$ otherwise. What is its DC value?
distractor_plan: Use the high level alone without duty-cycle weighting.
Use the complement $1-D$ instead of $D$.
Divide by the duty cycle instead of multiplying by it.
Add the levels instead of averaging them by time fraction.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic rectangular signal is $12$ for $\frac{1}{3}$ of each period and $0$ for the rest. What is its DC value?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Multiply the high level by the duty cycle and express the DC value as the one-period average.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The duty cycle is now given directly, so the learner only has to substitute into the average formula.
solution_step_plan: Identify the high level $12$, the low level $0$, and the duty cycle $D = \frac{1}{3}$.
Write the DC value as the weighted average $12\cdot\frac{1}{3} + 0\cdot\frac{2}{3}$.
Simplify the arithmetic to get the final DC value.
State the result as the average value over one period.
practice_variation_axes: Change the duty-cycle fraction.
Change the high level.
Use a decimal duty cycle instead of a fraction.
Keep the low level at $0$ so the learner focuses on the weighting.

sections.handoff_notes: Use five symbolic answer choices with one correct value. Keep the distractors algebraic rather than visual or conceptual.

sections.section_title: Finding Duty Cycle from Pulse Width and Period
sections.learning_goal: Convert pulse width and period into duty cycle before computing the DC value.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the pulse width, period, and levels are given symbolically in the text.

question_policy.answer_format: A single simplified symbolic value or fraction for the DC value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A rectangular signal has pulse width $\tau$ and period $T$. If the high level is $A$ and the low level is $0$, what is its DC value?
distractor_plan: Invert the ratio and use $T/\tau$ instead of $\tau/T$.
Treat the pulse width as the duty cycle directly.
Multiply by the period instead of by the duty cycle.
Ignore the low-level interval and use the high level alone.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A rectangular signal is high for $2$ ms of every $5$ ms period and is $0$ otherwise. If the high level is $10$, what is its DC value?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Read the pulse width and period, compute $D = \tau/T$, and then substitute into the average-value formula.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The duty cycle is not stated directly; the learner must derive it from the pulse width and period before averaging.
solution_step_plan: Read the pulse width $\tau = 2$ ms and the period $T = 5$ ms.
Convert the geometry into duty cycle $D = \tau/T = 2/5$.
Substitute the duty cycle into the on/off average with high level $10$ and low level $0$.
Simplify to the final DC value.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse width and period.
Change the high level.
Ask for a reduced fraction when the ratio simplifies.
Keep the low level at $0$ so the main task is duty-cycle conversion.

sections.handoff_notes: The practice item should still be one-answer multiple choice. The hidden skill is converting $\tau/T$ correctly before using the average.

sections.section_title: Computing DC Value for a Two-Level Rectangular Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute the DC value of a rectangular signal with two nonzero levels using a weighted average.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the two-level rectangular signal is specified symbolically.

question_policy.answer_format: A single simplified symbolic value or fraction for the DC value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic rectangular signal is $A_H$ for a fraction $D$ of each period and $A_L$ for the rest. What is its DC value?
distractor_plan: Use only the high level and ignore the low-level interval.
Use only the low level and ignore the high-level interval.
Average the two levels equally instead of weighting by time fraction.
Switch the weights $D$ and $1-D$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic rectangular signal is $6$ for $\frac{1}{4}$ of each period and $-1$ for the rest. What is its DC value?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Form the weighted average of the high and low levels and simplify the result.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The low level is no longer $0$, so the learner must weight both levels by their time fractions.
solution_step_plan: Identify the high level $6$, the low level $-1$, and the duty cycle $D = \frac{1}{4}$.
Write the weighted average $6\cdot\frac{1}{4} + (-1)\cdot\frac{3}{4}$.
Simplify the two contributions carefully.
State the final DC value.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the two levels.
Vary the duty cycle.
Use a negative low level with a positive high level.
Require fraction simplification after combining the weighted terms.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the first nonzero two-level average. Keep the worked example explicitly weighted, not shortcut by symmetry.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero DC Value from Balanced Signal Levels
sections.learning_goal: Recognize balanced weighted levels that force the DC value to be zero.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the balance condition is conveyed symbolically through the signal levels and time fractions.

question_policy.answer_format: A single simplified symbolic value or fraction for the DC value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic rectangular signal is $A_H$ for a fraction $D$ of each period and $A_L$ for the rest, with the two weighted contributions canceling exactly. What is its DC value?
distractor_plan: Average the magnitudes instead of the signed contributions.
Use the high level alone instead of the weighted average.
Use the low level alone instead of the weighted average.
Miss the cancellation and carry through a small nonzero arithmetic error.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic rectangular signal is $4$ for $\frac{1}{3}$ of each period and $-2$ for the rest. What is its DC value?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the positive and negative weighted contributions cancel exactly, so the DC value is zero.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The main task is no longer finding a nonzero average but spotting the balance condition that forces cancellation.
solution_step_plan: Write the weighted average using the two levels and their time fractions.
Show that the positive contribution and the negative contribution have equal magnitude.
Conclude that the weighted sum is zero.
State that no further arithmetic is needed once the cancellation is recognized.
practice_variation_axes: Use different balanced level pairs.
Use equal-half opposite-sign signals as a special case.
Ask for zero/nonzero recognition from the weighted-average condition.
Vary the fractions while keeping the contributions equal in magnitude.

sections.handoff_notes: End the lesson with recognition, not new algebra. The point is to spot when the weighted average cancels to zero.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify coefficient cancellations in the Fourier series coefficient formula to determine which even and odd harmonic indices of a periodic signal contribute nonzero spectral components.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Even and Odd Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Teach the parity test for Fourier-series coefficient formulas so the writer can show how $(-1)^k$ splits even and odd harmonic indices into surviving and vanishing sets.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson is symbolic and only requires parity checks on Fourier coefficients.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions for a tutorial section.

sections.section_title: Plotting Positive and Negative Harmonic Magnitudes

sections.section_title: Interpreting Harmonic Strengths from a Magnitude Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Read a magnitude spectrum stem plot as a harmonic-strength distribution and identify the dominant and missing harmonics.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A centered magnitude-spectrum stem plot with one dominant DC stem, one smaller harmonic pair, and one zero-magnitude harmonic position so the learner can interpret the harmonic strength distribution.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the plot uncluttered and make the relative stem heights easy to compare. Use one clearly tallest stem, one medium pair, and one absent harmonic so the interpretation task has a single clear answer.

question_policy.answer_format: conceptual interpretation of the spectrum
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a magnitude spectrum stem plot, which statement correctly identifies the strongest harmonic and any missing harmonics?

Ignore the DC stem when comparing harmonic strength.

ask for the strongest component or the missing component

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute and interpret the phase spectrum by extracting the argument of each nonzero complex Fourier series coefficient and aligning those phases with the corresponding positive and negative harmonics of a periodic continuous-time signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Phase Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Define the phase spectrum as the list of arguments $\phi_k = \arg(C_k)$ attached to each harmonic index and show how it extends the magnitude spectrum with angle information.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the learner to read phase as $\phi_k = \arg(C_k)$ from each complex Fourier coefficient and attach that phase to the correct harmonic index $k$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one nonzero coefficient, such as $C_1 = 3e^{-j\pi/4}$, so the learner sees a single phase entry before any harmonic pairing or zero handling.
paragraph_plan: Reframe the magnitude spectrum as only half of the picture: the phase spectrum records the angle of each complex coefficient.
Show the polar-form rule $C_k = |C_k|e^{j\phi_k}$ and read $\phi_k = \arg(C_k)$ as the phase at harmonic $k$.
Apply the rule to the one-coefficient base case and place the phase at the matching harmonic index instead of treating phase as a separate object.
Close with the real-signal reminder that conjugate harmonic pairs carry opposite phases and zero coefficients have no defined phase entry.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening definition-first and stay inside symbolic coefficient notation; do not add practice to the tutorial step.

sections.section_title: Extracting Phase from a Nonzero Complex Coefficient
sections.learning_goal: Extract the principal argument of one nonzero complex coefficient and report it as the phase at the given harmonic index.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices giving candidate principal phase values in radians for the specified harmonic coefficient.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given one complex coefficient in rectangular form, choose the correct principal phase at the stated harmonic index.
distractor_plan: Use the reference angle with the wrong sign.
Pick the angle from the wrong quadrant.
Confuse magnitude with phase.
Shift by $\pi/2$ or $\pi$ as a common quadrant mistake.
Attach the phase to the wrong harmonic index.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $C_2 = -1 - \sqrt{3}j$, compute the phase at harmonic $k=2$ and rewrite the coefficient in phase-angle form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert a rectangular coefficient to polar form, extract the principal argument, and report the phase-spectrum value for the named harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial defined phase from polar form; this example gives the coefficient in rectangular form so the learner must determine the angle from the signs and quadrant.
solution_step_plan: Locate $C_2$ on the complex plane and identify the correct quadrant.
Determine the principal argument $\phi_2$ from the real and imaginary parts.
State the phase-spectrum entry at $k=2$.
Optionally rewrite $C_2$ as $|C_2|e^{j\phi_2}$ to confirm the angle.
practice_variation_axes: Change the coefficient magnitude while keeping the same quadrant.
Move the coefficient to a different quadrant so the phase sign changes.
Swap the harmonic index so the phase must be attached to a different $k$.
Require the learner to choose between equivalent angles such as $-\pi/3$ and $5\pi/3$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as the first single-coefficient extraction problem; the later question generator should mirror the one-harmonic structure with five symbolic answer choices.

sections.section_title: Assigning Phases to Positive and Negative Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Map each nonzero coefficient to its harmonic index and assign the matching phase to both positive and negative harmonics.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices showing candidate phase tables or phase assignments by harmonic index.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a small coefficient table, choose the phase assignment that correctly matches positive and negative harmonic indices.

example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example handled one coefficient; this one adds multiple harmonic indices, a DC term, and a mirrored negative harmonic so the learner must keep index, sign, and phase aligned across a table.
solution_step_plan: List the nonzero coefficients and read off each argument.
Place $\phi_k$ at the matching positive or negative harmonic index.
Record the DC phase at $k=0$.

sections.handoff_notes: Use a compact coefficient table and make the index-to-phase alignment explicit; the later MCQ should test harmonic placement rather than algebraic manipulation.

sections.section_title: Leaving Zero Coefficients Out of the Phase Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Exclude zero coefficients from the phase spectrum instead of assigning them a phase value.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices identifying the correct set of harmonic indices that should appear in the phase spectrum.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a coefficient table with zeros, choose the phase-spectrum support that omits the zero coefficients.
distractor_plan: Assign phase $0$ to a zero coefficient.
Infer a phase from neighboring harmonics.
Include the zero coefficients as blank phase entries.
Omit the wrong harmonic index.
Treat zero magnitude as if it implied a special phase value.

Mark their phase as undefined and exclude them from the phase spectrum.
Keep only the nonzero harmonics in the final phase list.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Phase Spectrum from Fourier Coefficients
sections.learning_goal: Compute a full phase spectrum from a coefficient table and interpret which harmonics are present, absent, and phase-shifted.

question_policy.answer_format: Five text choices giving candidate full phase-spectrum tables for the listed harmonic indices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a full coefficient table, choose the phase-spectrum table that combines the DC term, nonzero harmonic phases, and omitted zero harmonics.
distractor_plan: Flip the sign of one conjugate pair.
Treat the negative DC term as phase $0$ instead of $\pi$.
Insert a phase entry for the zero pair.
Swap the phases of $k=1$ and $k=3$.
Use magnitudes as if they were phases.

Omit the zero coefficients entirely from the phase list.
